lesson.title: Right Type, Wrong Value: Understanding ValueError
lesson.summary: ValueError means the type of a value was completely acceptable for the operation, but the specific value inside it was not something the operation could actually work with.
lesson.body:
The last chapter established TypeError as what happens when the kind of thing you have does not match what an operation needs at all. ValueError is the other exception beginners run into constantly, and it is the mirror image: the type is exactly right, the operation has no complaint about that, but the particular value held inside that correctly typed object is not something the operation can actually handle.

The clearest examples come from type conversion. int() is documented to accept a string and convert it to an integer, so passing it a str is never, by itself, a type problem. But int() can only succeed if that string actually spells out a whole number in digits.

```python
user_input = "twenty"
age = int(user_input)
```

Running this prints a traceback whose final line is:

```
ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'twenty'
```

Compare this to the TypeError example from the last chapter. There, age + 1 failed because a str can never be added to an int, full stop, regardless of what the string said. Here, int(user_input) is being asked to do something it is perfectly able to do with a string, plenty of other strings work fine, int("20") returns the int 20 without any trouble. The failure here is specific to this value: the characters "twenty" simply do not spell a base 10 integer, so int() has no digits to convert, and it raises ValueError rather than silently guessing or returning something meaningless.

ValueError shows up outside of type conversion too, always following the same pattern of a right type carrying a wrong value. Calling [1, 2, 3].remove(5) is a good example: remove() expects an item to search for and delete, and 5 is a perfectly ordinary int, exactly the type remove() is built to accept, but 5 does not happen to be present in this particular list, so there is nothing valid for remove() to do, and it raises ValueError: list.remove(x): x not in list.

Holding TypeError and ValueError side by side is one of the most useful habits you can build as a beginner, because both are extremely common and the fix for each is different. TypeError means you need to change the type you are working with, often with a conversion function like int(), float(), or str(). ValueError means the type was already correct, and instead you need to check, or ask for, a different specific value, something conversion alone cannot fix, since no amount of type conversion turns "twenty" into a number int() can parse. This distinction matters especially whenever you convert input typed by an actual person, since people can type anything at all, and a ValueError from a mismatched conversion is one of the single most common exceptions you will encounter in real, working programs.
